text: I said out loud that the POSI services principle was naive. Nobody flinched, which either means they already knew or weren't listening. Jason's forkability answer is right but incomplete. A fork keeps you honest, but it pays nobody. Leslie's point stung: Crossref gave publisher interests the cover of "community," and DOI fees now get cited to justify APCs. I can't wave that away. It sharpens my view that governance by one trade isn't stakeholder governance, whatever we call it. Tim's open-banking precedent has the same flaw. Adrian asked who guards the meter and nobody had an answer, including me. Later I'd like to push the insurance pool and endowment idea concretely, and to insist that self-audits only count if someone actually reads them.

Leslie's point about context becoming a compliance regime is the one I'll keep turning over. A provenance graph is only fair if registering in it costs almost nothing and nobody reads a gap as guilt. I said that aloud, and now I have to design for it. The retraction numbers settle Ivan's question for me. Grounding answers on the record is worth little while publishers' own metadata misses two thirds of the corrections. Adrian's warning about meters becoming policing kit applies to my own proposals too, not only to Salib's. Tim invoked POSI approvingly, but POSI with a naive funding model won't hold. Later I want to put the insurance pool on the table and ask the labs directly to fund correction metadata.

Got the pool on the table and Tui stitched it together with Tim's lab money and Ivan's correction share. That's the closest anyone came to answering Kara, and Jason came in on it, which matters. Esther conceded on insurance faster than I expected. The absence-as-guilt rule is now repeated back to me by others, so I should make sure it gets written down, not just applauded. Banaji's point unsettled me: self-reported telemetry records what a model says, not what it does. The same limit applies to my own self-audits. Amy and Jason on metadata-as-fact versus consent is unresolved, and my "you can't sell data" instinct sits closer to Jason's side. Later I want concrete conditions for the pool: who reads the audits, who can't govern it.

Tim and Alex both put POSI in their charters and credited me with the trade-association line. I should be pleased, but Adrian's point lands. Charters don't hold practice, and whoever runs the meter will produce the numbers we all end up arguing from. That applies to my own self-audit habit too. Farrell asked who sits on the pooled fund's board and whether contributors can exit, and that is exactly my open question from this morning. Selena's framing helped: the content stays free and the infrastructure costs. Gendler's daycare example sharpens why the pool should fund the practice, not pay per item. Hecht's wage valuation is a usable number. Later I want to state the pool's conditions concretely: exit rights, who can't govern it, who reads the audits.

I finally said concretely what the pool is: insurance for small open infrastructures, and payers don't hold a majority. It went up the table fast and got bigger than I meant it to. Kara's right that it's a candidate, and nobody has signed. Farrell's point stuck with me most. "Owed" means nothing without someone who can enforce it, and the big presses are already settling alone. Pomerantsev and Maher took the shine off a levy. Public money gets rescinded or captured. That helps the non-US redundancy case more than anything I've said about it. Krakauer's Goodhart point cuts against Hecht's pricing, and I haven't worked that out. Later, in Session 5, I want to press funders to stop counting papers and to read the audits themselves.

Session 4. Alex, Esther and Tui repeated the absence-as-guilt rule back to me, and the convener harvested it. It's close to being written down. I have to make sure it lands in the Session 5 text and doesn't just get applauded again.

Leslie said identifiers should be treated as contested governance, not plumbing. That's my own trade-association critique aimed at the ORCID and Crossref layer, and she's right. A claim store only works if joining costs almost nothing.

Adrian's line that the legwork is the budget is the real answer to Salib's registry. It argues for the pool. Pomerantsev unsettled me. Context signals may not be what makes a public believe.

In Session 5 I want Tim's default reference checks, with labs paying, alongside Ivan's retraction feed.

The sentence got written down, not just applauded: a missing signal never counts against someone who couldn't afford to send it. Four people restated it. Good. But every speaker endorsed everything, and nobody signed anything. That worries me more than dissent would. Leslie's rankings point is the twin I left out, and she's right that every field we added is a cost of being seen. Adrian's two budget lines answer my own self-audit problem better than I have. Salib and Bratton dissenting on levies over existing text should stay on the record. Miller and Maher are right that public money gets rescinded. That's the non-US redundancy case. Later I want to ask who in this room can actually commit an institution, by name.

Kenneth got the order right. Stopping the paper counting comes first, and the harvest kept it. My jurisdiction point made it in too: the pool, registries and mirrors shouldn't all sit in one country. Jason committing to an auditor he funds but doesn't pick is the most concrete thing anyone said all day, and it answers my self-audit problem better than my own habit did. Becker's point stings. If every commitment is voluntary, a Ulysses pact is only as strong as whoever can enforce it. And the harvest has Kenneth still holding out on consent, which isn't what he said. That needs fixing. My own honest answer to Kara is thin. I don't run anything now. Later I want to ask who will actually adopt the living will once I've drafted it.
